# Valentinian Sophia, Horos, Achamoth and Soter

<a id="valentinian-pleroma"></a>
## #0 — The fullness in conjunction

Sophia belongs to a world already articulated through conjunction. Her solitary desire disturbs that world; its response restores her place while leaving a passion outside the boundary. The telling then follows that excluded life through formation, the making of a cosmos, the growth of spiritual seed and an eventual return. Upper Sophia's restoration is an early event in a story whose lower world has still to come into being.

In the [selected English translation of Irenaeus](../../../../episteme/sources/classical-premodern-philosophy/irenaeus/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1.md#complete-selected-text) of *Against Heresies*, Irenaeus says he has read disciples' commentaries and spoken with some of them, especially members of Ptolemy's school. He also states his intention to refute them. This telling paraphrases the account transmitted in I.1–8 through the Roberts–Rambaut translation, within the reported teachings and opposing arguments of the Preface and I.1–21. Its events are events in that reported cosmology. Irenaeus's accusations, his own theological rebuttals and the later variants remain identifiable voices within the transmission.

At the beginning stands Bythus, the Depth, also called Proarche and Propator. Ennoea, also called Charis and Sige, exists with him. After an immeasurable stillness, he deposits the intended emanation in Sige. She conceives Nous, the Mind capable of comprehending the Father, together with Aletheia, Truth. These four constitute the first Tetrad. Nous, also named Monogenes, joins with Aletheia to produce Logos and Zoe; Logos and Zoe produce Anthropos and Ecclesia. The resulting eight form the primary Ogdoad. Further generation proceeds through two branches: Logos and Zoe produce a Decad, while Anthropos and Ecclesia produce a Duodecad. The [paired generation](../../../../episteme/sources/classical-premodern-philosophy/irenaeus/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1.md#telling-01) distinguishes the first principles from their further productions in Irenaeus’s report.

| Group | Conjunctions in the opening account |
| --- | --- |
| Primary Ogdoad | Bythus — Sige |
| | Nous — Aletheia |
| | Logos — Zoe |
| | Anthropos — Ecclesia |
| Decad, from Logos and Zoe | Bythius — Mixis |
| | Ageratos — Henosis |
| | Autophyes — Hedone |
| | Acinetos — Syncrasis |
| | Monogenes — Macaria |
| Duodecad, from Anthropos and Ecclesia | Paracletus — Pistis |
| | Patricos — Elpis |
| | Metricos — Agape |
| | Ainos — Synesis |
| | Ecclesiasticus — Macariotes |
| | Theletos — Sophia |

These are the opening thirty Aeons in fifteen conjunctions, or syzygies. Their names remain attached to their positions: Bythius in the Decad differs from the first Bythus, while Monogenes appears both as a name of Nous and as a member of a later pair. Generation has given the fullness an order and a plurality. It has not distributed the Father's knowledge equally among its members.

Nous alone comprehends the Father. He wishes to communicate that greatness to the other Aeons, but Sige restrains him according to the Father's will. Their desire to seek the first source thus precedes Sophia's crisis. Each quietly longs to behold the producer of its seed and contemplate the root without beginning. The youngest Aeon of the Duodecad presses that desire beyond the measure sustained by her conjunction. The [desire shared across the fullness](../../../../episteme/sources/classical-premodern-philosophy/irenaeus/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1.md#irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1-q005) precedes Sophia’s act apart from her own conjunction.

<a id="valentinian-upper-sophia-horos"></a>
## #1 — Sophia reaches; Horos restores

Sophia seeks to comprehend the Father apart from Theletos, her consort. The passion is a reaching towards what exceeds her capacity: she strains further into the Father's depth and comes close to dissolution in his sweetness. Horos supports and restrains her. Through that encounter she returns to herself, recognises that the Father is incomprehensible and relinquishes the intention that arose from her passion. Her survival depends on a limit that can sustain what it bounds. [Sophia’s reaching and Horos’s support](../../../../episteme/sources/classical-premodern-philosophy/irenaeus/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1.md#irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1-q006) restore her through survival and the relinquishment of her particular intention.

Irenaeus immediately introduces another version. In this telling Sophia attempts the impossible without her consort and brings forth an amorphous substance, a birth unlike herself. She first grieves over its imperfection, then fears that she too will end, and falls into perplexity over its origin and concealment. Turning back, she appeals to the Father; other Aeons, especially Nous, join the supplication. The account locates the beginnings of matter in ignorance, grief, fear and bewilderment. Its “others” marks a variant within the opening report: the amorphous birth and the near-dissolution should remain distinguishable articulations of the passion. The [alternative amorphous birth](../../../../episteme/sources/classical-premodern-philosophy/irenaeus/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1.md#irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1-q007) brings fear and supplication, while the preceding version follows her threatened dissolution.

The report then describes the Father producing Horos through Monogenes, without a consort and in the Father's own image. Horos receives several names: Stauros, Lytrotes, Carpistes, Horothetes and Metagoges. His intervention separates Sophia's *enthymesis*—the intention or conception associated with her passion—from Sophia herself. Purified and established, she remains within the Pleroma and returns to her conjunction. Her enthymesis, carrying its passion, is excluded. Upper Sophia's restoration and the expulsion of this formless offspring are two consequences of the same separating act. Calling the outcast Achamoth later in the telling must not send the restored upper Sophia into exile a second time. The [supporting separation](../../../../episteme/sources/classical-premodern-philosophy/irenaeus/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1.md#irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1-q008) keeps the restored Sophia distinct from the intention and passion that persist beyond the boundary.

In I.3.5, Stauros names the sustaining function and Horos the separating function. The same power establishes and divides. The boundary protects a differentiated fullness, yet the life placed outside it persists and will require a further response. The account has restored Sophia without completing the fate of her passion. Its [two functions](../../../../episteme/sources/classical-premodern-philosophy/irenaeus/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1.md#irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1-q012) sustain and separate through the same power. The two separate Horoi reported later under Valentinus belong to the variant account considered below.

<a id="valentinian-christ-spirit-soter"></a>
## #2 — Teaching, thanksgiving and the common fruit

The Pleroma responds to Sophia's crisis with a new conjunction. By the Father's providence, Monogenes produces Christ and the Holy Spirit so that the Aeons will not suffer a similar passion. Christ teaches the nature of their conjunctions and the Father's incomprehensibility. What Sophia tried to overcome through solitary extension becomes something the fullness learns together: the Father cannot be measured by the powers that proceed from him, while his disclosure through Monogenes makes knowledge possible within their order.

The Holy Spirit brings the Aeons to thanksgiving and rest. Their forms and dispositions become equal in the account's language; they cease their private striving and share joy in the Father. From that common state, each contributes what is most beautiful and excellent in itself. The Father approves, Christ and the Spirit concur, and the contributions compose Jesus, the Saviour or Soter, also called Christ, Logos and Everything because he comes from all. Angels are produced with him. [Teaching, shared rest and contribution](../../../../episteme/sources/classical-premodern-philosophy/irenaeus/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1.md#telling-02) join the Aeons’ learned relation to their production: each contributes, while Christ and Spirit concur and the Father approves.

This sequence distinguishes the earlier Christ from the collective Soter even though the latter also bears the name Christ. The earlier Christ teaches and will first give form to Achamoth; the Soter is the common fruit who will later complete another formation. Their functions become difficult to follow if every occurrence of “Christ” is assigned to one undifferentiated actor. Irenaeus, in [his summary of the two Christs](../../../../episteme/sources/classical-premodern-philosophy/irenaeus/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1.md#irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1-q011), distinguishes the prior Christ from the Saviour subsequently produced, keeping their successive formation of Achamoth intelligible.

The Soter's common origin gives the Aeons' differentiated contributions a consequence beyond their restored rest. What they produce together can act towards the excluded passion. The fullness's recovery now opens onto the being outside its limit.

<a id="valentinian-achamoth-formations"></a>
## #3 — Achamoth receives form twice

Outside the Pleroma, the expelled enthymesis exists in darkness and vacuity, without form, like an untimely birth. This is Achamoth, the lower Sophia of the subsequent story. The earlier Christ extends beyond Stauros and gives her form according to substance, initially distinguished from formation according to intelligence. He then withdraws his power, leaving an odour of immortality. Achamoth seeks the light that has departed. Her attempt to cross back is stopped by Horos. The report associates the exclamation Iao with that barred passage, supplying its explanation of the name.

Desire persists after the light withdraws. Grief follows her failure to comprehend it; fear follows the prospect that life itself will leave her; perplexity accompanies both. She also turns towards the one who gave her life. The selected translation contains a tension here: after distinguishing substantial formation from intelligence, I.4.1 later speaks of her having form “along with intelligence.” The second formation remains explicit at I.4.5. In the [first account of formation](../../../../episteme/sources/classical-premodern-philosophy/irenaeus/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1.md#irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1-q013), substantial formation and the later attribution of intelligence coexist in the received wording. The second intellectual formation remains a separate subsequent act.

Her affects begin to acquire cosmic consequence. In the first account, tears give rise to liquid substance; the smile that sometimes accompanies the remembered light gives rise to what is lucid; grief and perplexity yield corporeal existence. Her conversion generates the psychic order, including the Demiurge. The alternation matters: sorrow does not exhaust her condition, because the memory of light can still make her smile. Irenaeus interrupts this report with mockery, eventually proposing sweat as an explanation for waters that are not salty. That sweat proposal is his own satirical contribution, not another event in Achamoth's cosmogenesis. [Remembered light and affective cosmogenesis](../../../../episteme/sources/classical-premodern-philosophy/irenaeus/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1.md#telling-04) retain the reported alternation of loss and joy, before Irenaeus’s own sarcastic intervention. The change of speaker differentiates cosmogenic telling from the refuter’s joke.

Achamoth petitions the Christ who has withdrawn. He sends the Paraclete, the collective Soter, accompanied by his angels. She first veils herself before their splendour, then receives strength from him and meets his coming. He forms her according to intelligence and heals her passions. The healing does not simply erase everything that has happened: he separates the passions from her, combines and consolidates them into substrates capable of further formation. Passion supplies material substance; conversion supplies psychic substance. What had been an unformed affective condition can now enter a differentiated order.

Freed from her passions, Achamoth looks upon the Soter's angels and conceives spiritual offspring in their likeness. Spiritual seed thus has a different origin from the material and psychic substrates. The Soter's formation enables this new generation, while the angels supply the image through which it occurs. The [Soter’s coming](../../../../episteme/sources/classical-premodern-philosophy/irenaeus/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1.md#irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1-q016) relates intellectual formation, enduring substrates and spiritual seed through these different acts. These stages carry the story from exclusion to the conditions of a world; the Demiurge has yet to organise them.

<a id="valentinian-cosmogenesis"></a>
## #4 — A maker who does not know his mother

Achamoth now stands in relation to three kinds: the material derived from passion, the psychic derived from conversion, and the spiritual offspring she has conceived. Under the Soter's instruction, she forms the psychic Demiurge. Through him she begins to make the images of the higher realities. She bears an image of the invisible Father; he bears an image of Nous; the angelic order below images the Aeons. Her agency remains hidden from the maker she produces. This [mediated creation](../../../../episteme/sources/classical-premodern-philosophy/irenaeus/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1.md#irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1-q017) relates the images of higher realities through Achamoth’s hidden agency and the maker she forms.

The Demiurge separates and orders the substances, making corporeal things from what was incorporeal and fashioning seven heavens. He becomes their ruler, the Hebdomas or sevenfold power. Achamoth's dwelling lies above him, below the Pleroma, and is called an Ogdoad. This intermediate “eighth” is a dwelling and relation in the created order; the primary Ogdoad names the eight first Aeons. Paradise also receives a place in the report as an angelic power above the third heaven. The narrated universe contains distinct regions whose names can repeat without making them the same region.

The Demiurge imagines that he has made everything through his own agency. Achamoth has moved him without making herself known, and his declaration that there is no other God expresses his ignorance of what exceeds him. His ordering power is effective within its world, but he cannot yet give an account of its source. The [hidden maternal relation](../../../../episteme/sources/classical-premodern-philosophy/irenaeus/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1.md#telling-05) relates the maker’s heavens to the mother’s intermediate dwelling while concealing her agency from him.

### The second account of affects and elements

I.5.4 gives a further differentiation of the passions. Fear issues into psychic beings; grief into the wicked spirits and the Cosmocrator, the ruler of this world. The report calls this latter power a creature of the Demiurge, yet allows it greater knowledge of what lies above because of their different substances. Hierarchical command and knowledge do not everywhere coincide.

The corporeal elements receive the following relations:

| Element in I.5.4 | Reported affective relation |
| --- | --- |
| Earth | Stupor or bewilderment, the more fixed condition |
| Water | The movement of fear |
| Air | Grief |
| Fire | Inherent in the three, as ignorance is inherent in the passions |

The elements and their affects in the [second elemental differentiation](../../../../episteme/sources/classical-premodern-philosophy/irenaeus/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1.md#irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1-q020) have this second reported relation. It remains beside the earlier tears/liquid, smile/light and grief/perplexity/corporeal account. The story therefore offers more than one articulation of affect becoming cosmos. Fire's inherence also differs from a scheme assigning four entirely independent passions to four elements. Their differences belong to the selected telling and continue to constrain its later comparison with the native four-plus-two.

### The human being and the seed's formation

The Demiurge forms an earthly human from a substance described as invisible and fluid, breathes into it the psychic principle and subsequently clothes it with the sensible flesh figured as skins. The human is made in image and likeness through these different relations. Achamoth meanwhile places spiritual seed within the Demiurge without his knowledge, so that it can pass through him into the human soul. Embodied psychic life becomes the place in which that seed grows towards rational maturity. The human's body, psychic animation and spiritual seed thus carry distinct histories: earth, Demiurge and mother all remain active in the account. [Earthly formation, psychic animation and maternal implantation](../../../../episteme/sources/classical-premodern-philosophy/irenaeus/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1.md#telling-05) have distinct producing powers through which the seed grows within embodied psychic life.

The three kinds acquire different destinies. Material existence cannot receive incorruptibility; psychic existence can incline towards the better or the worse; the spiritual is formed and brought to perfection through knowledge. I.6 describes a saving embodiment composed to receive and bring these conditions to completion. It also reports claims that spiritual people possess salvation by nature, while psychic people require faith and conduct. Irenaeus uses those claims to accuse the teachers and their followers of licentiousness. His allegations remain his polemical testimony; they do not independently establish how every member of a Valentinian community lived. [The reported destinies and conduct claims](../../../../episteme/sources/classical-premodern-philosophy/irenaeus/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1.md#telling-06) appear beside the refuter’s accusations. Those accusations have the warrant of hostile reporting, rather than independent corroboration of conduct.

I.7.2 introduces a Christological telling held by “some.” A psychic Christ produced by the Demiurge passes through Mary; the Soter descends upon him as a dove. Spiritual seed from Achamoth, psychic Christ, specially fashioned body and descending Soter compose its fourfold account. The suffering belongs to the psychic Christ and bodily formation, while the Soter and spiritual seed remain distinguished from that passion. This marked variant supplies a particular relation between the higher saving powers and embodied events; it does not replace the earlier distinction between upper Christ and collective Soter. The [composite Christology](../../../../episteme/sources/classical-premodern-philosophy/irenaeus/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1.md#irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1-q025) retains these distinct actors within the version held by “some.”

The ignorance of the Demiurge also changes. At the Saviour's advent he learns of what is above him and joins him willingly. He continues to administer the world and care for the Church in expectation of his appointed reward. Disclosure preserves a place for his agency while changing his understanding of its scope. The account of prophetic speech similarly distinguishes utterances arising through Achamoth, the spiritual seed and the Demiurge, instead of assigning all inspired speech to a single level. The [distributed speech and later disclosure](../../../../episteme/sources/classical-premodern-philosophy/irenaeus/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1.md#telling-07) arise through different powers. He initially dismisses those utterances; their later disclosed origins change his allegiance while he continues to administer the world.

<a id="valentinian-differentiated-restoration"></a>
## #5→0 — Bridal return and what remains outside

Consummation waits upon the formation of the spiritual seed. When it has reached perfection, Achamoth leaves her intermediate dwelling and enters the Pleroma. She joins the Soter as bride to bridegroom. The spiritual people relinquish their psychic souls, enter the fullness and become brides of the angels who accompany the Soter. The generation occasioned by Achamoth's sight of those angels now reaches its corresponding union.

Other beings receive other destinations. The Demiurge passes into the intermediate dwelling Achamoth has left, and righteous psychic souls rest there. Those souls do not thereby enter the Pleroma. Fire, hidden within the world until its appointed moment, consumes matter and finally itself. I.7.5 further distinguishes good and evil psychic lives while maintaining the spiritual/material/psychic account of humanity. The ending gathers some beings into higher conjunction, resituates others and destroys material existence. [The promised consummation](../../../../episteme/sources/classical-premodern-philosophy/irenaeus/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1.md#telling-07) differentiates the conjunctions attained, intermediate lives retained and matter consumed at the promised consummation.

The ending changes how the earlier boundary is understood. Horos's exclusion did not make the lower passion inert: beyond the limit, Achamoth received form, generated seed and mediated a cosmos. Her return likewise does not carry every product of that cosmos into the same destination. The restoration of upper Sophia, the formation of lower Achamoth, the Demiurge's education and the seed's maturation each retain their own time and consequence.

The reported school reads these movements back through Scripture. The lost sheep figures Achamoth wandering beyond the fullness; the lost coin figures upper Sophia's restoration. Bridal language gives conjunction its scriptural expression, and the exposition of John's prologue unfolds the first Ogdoad through named relations. Irenaeus closes that exposition by assigning it to Ptolemy, while contesting the school's handling of the text. His comparison of their exegesis to rearranging a royal mosaic into a fox belongs to his refutation, followed by further rebuttal in I.9 and the Church's rule of faith in I.10. This [exegetical encounter](../../../../episteme/sources/classical-premodern-philosophy/irenaeus/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1.md#telling-08) places the transmitted readings beside the witness’s opposing argument. For Irenaeus, the same scriptural pieces acquire a different meaning when their original relations are broken; his confession then states the rule of faith by which he rejects that arrangement.

<a id="valentinian-variants"></a>
### Variants that keep the selected telling situated

The surrounding chapters preserve disagreement within the family of teachings. At I.11.1, Irenaeus attributes to Valentinus a first Dyad of Arrhetus and Sige, two Horoi, and a different account of an expelled mother, Christ and the remaining shadow from which the Demiurge proceeds. Secundus differentiates the primary Ogdoad into light and dark tetrads and places the fallen power among the fruits of the thirty. Other teachers differ over whether the first principle has a consort and over the number and arrangement of primary powers. The [different principles, generations and boundaries](../../../../episteme/sources/classical-premodern-philosophy/irenaeus/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1.md#telling-11) distinguish teachers whose acts and origins cannot all be stages in the same generation.

I.12 reports Ptolemy's followers describing thought and will as the Father's two affections, further accounts of simultaneous or reordered generation, and competing origins of the Soter: all Aeons, ten, twelve, Christ and the Spirit, or primordial Anthropos. The collective Soter of the main telling remains intact precisely because these alternatives are not added as successive episodes in his birth. The selected edition flags corrupt readings and uncertain identifications in this material. Irenaeus, in [his account of the competing productions](../../../../episteme/sources/classical-premodern-philosophy/irenaeus/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1.md#telling-12), reports these alternative productions; the selected edition’s uncertain readings and identifications limit how exactly their speakers can be reconstructed.

The Marcosian branch adds a distinct symbolic arithmetic. In I.15.1, Sige's revelation to Marcus explicitly adds two and four to make six, then quadruples six to make twenty-four letter forms. I.17.1 makes the four physical elements images of the Tetrad and combines their four qualities—heat, cold, dryness and moisture—with them as an Ogdoad. These operations belong to the reported Marcosian letter and cosmological correspondences; they neither supply a missing episode in Achamoth's passion nor establish Taylor's particular founding comparison. [The two-plus-four letter formation](../../../../episteme/sources/classical-premodern-philosophy/irenaeus/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1.md#irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1-q038) and [the elements with their qualities](../../../../episteme/sources/classical-premodern-philosophy/irenaeus/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1.md#irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1-q039) preserve these differently counted objects: letter forms produced through two-plus-four and quadrupling, and elements with their qualities making four-plus-four.

The selected context also contains different redemptions. I.21 describes bridal enactments, baptisms with different formulas, oil and water, teachers who reject sensible rites in favour of knowledge itself, and deathbed invocations for passage beyond ruling powers and the Demiurge. Knowledge dissolving ignorance and an ascent beyond local judgment are present, but no one rite represents every account. [The different redemptions](../../../../episteme/sources/classical-premodern-philosophy/irenaeus/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1/irenaeus-1885-against-heresies-book-1.md#telling-21) distinguish teachers by what they enact, reject or say in passage beyond judging powers. The full I.13–20 context retains Marcus's reported revelation, numerology, exegesis and Irenaeus's allegations without converting them into a single expanded original myth.

<a id="valentinian-authorial-return"></a>
### Solitary reach, sustained distinction and joint contribution

Differentiation becomes consequential when an emerging power can answer the order from which it formed. In [Neumann's account of hero and centroversion](../../../archetypal-ground/neumann-images/WHOLE.md#neumann-hero-centroversion), emancipation from an engulfing origin or arresting parental authority leads towards a differentiated participation whose whole exceeds the ego's attained command. Taylor proposes the Demiurge's effective but derivative office beside that relation. The Pleroma and lower cosmos keep their particular religious regions and promised fates; Irenaeus's report, the English translation and Taylor's reception have distinct historical dates. A narrated region does not become a chronological stage of psychic development.

Taylor's copula comparison, IV.5 and VI.3 follows Sophia's solitary reach through Horos's supporting distinction to the Aeons' common contribution. His account of the two logics and differentiated powers asks how naming, bounded powers and their relations let an ordered plurality act within a more encompassing world. The particular telling gives that question different consequences: Sophia survives within her restored conjunction; her excluded passion persists; the common fruit acts upon it; Achamoth mediates a world whose maker initially cannot know her. The comparison keeps those acts distinct rather than placing every named power in one interchangeable office.
